intro: Imperia's remarkable trees are mostly in the hill villages behind it, by churches and on mountain passes, and you need a car for most of them. Seven are on this map, all from Italy's national list of monumental trees: a Bunya pine in Imperia itself, a hackberry at Diano Borello, downy oaks at Maro Castello, a holm oak at the Lampedusa sanctuary in Castellaro, horse chestnuts at two churches in Triora, and a sweet chestnut eight and a half metres round on the Passo Furchè above Ceriana.
meta_description: Monumental trees around Imperia: a giant chestnut above Ceriana, a holm oak at Castellaro, oaks in Borgomaro and the horse chestnuts of Triora.
question_answer: No reliable age is published for any of these trees. By size the likeliest oldest is the sweet chestnut on the Passo Furchè above Ceriana, 8.5 metres round on the national list; a mountain-bike guide calls it 1,300 years old, which nobody has measured. A trunk that size could be several centuries old.
question_meta: No reliable age is published. By size the likeliest oldest is the sweet chestnut on the Passo Furchè above Ceriana, 8.5 metres round.
question_context: These trees spread over the valleys behind Imperia rather than one town, so plan them as drives. The Bunya pine stands in Imperia itself, on Viale Matteotti at the Palazzo della Provincia. Five kilometres inland, the hackberry stands on the cobbled churchyard of San Michele Arcangelo at Diano Borello, and up the Impero valley the two downy oaks grow at Maro Castello in the commune of Borgomaro. The big chestnut is the most remote: it grows on the Passo Furchè, on a mountain ridge above Ceriana, up a long climb and a dirt road, and it is the one to plan a day around. Triora, high in the Argentina valley, has two tall listed horse chestnuts by the church of Sant'Agostino and a third at San Bernardino; Castellaro's holm oak stands at the Lampedusa sanctuary. All seven stand by churches or sanctuaries, on a public street or on open mountain land, and none charges entry, though for the oaks at Maro Castello we could not confirm whether the meadow they grow in is open, so look from the lane.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree near Imperia?
faq.a: No source gives a reliable age. The biggest trunk belongs to the sweet chestnut on the Passo Furchè above Ceriana, 8.5 metres round on the national list. A mountain-bike guide calls it 1,300 years old; nobody has measured, so we leave its age open.
For most of them, yes. The Bunya pine is in Imperia itself, but the others are in hill villages with few buses, and the Ceriana chestnut is at the end of a long dirt road over a mountain ridge.

faq.q: Which trees are closest to Pontedassio?
faq.a: The hackberry at the church of Diano Borello and the downy oaks at Maro Castello in Borgomaro, each about five kilometres away as the crow flies. The Bunya pine in Imperia is about seven.

Yes. They stand by churches, on a public street and on open mountain land. For the oaks at Maro Castello we could not confirm whether the meadow they grow in is open, so look from the lane if in doubt.

trees.name: The Bunya Pine of the Palazzo della Provincia

location.address: Palazzo della Provincia, Viale Giacomo Matteotti 147, Imperia

trees.story:
The cones of this tree can weigh up to about ten kilograms, which is why people in Australia are told not to park under one. This Bunya pine on Viale Matteotti in Imperia is 26 metres tall and 3.45 metres round, according to Italy's national list of monumental trees, and it is the only one of the province's listed trees in the city itself.

The Bunya pine comes from the rainforests of south-east Queensland, where Aboriginal peoples gathered in great numbers for the bunya nut harvest. It reached European gardens in the nineteenth century and suits the Riviera, where frost is rare. You can tell it from the palms and pines around it by its shape: a straight trunk carrying a dense dome of stiff, prickly, glossy leaves arranged in whorls, more like a giant candelabra than a pine.

It stands at the Palazzo della Provincia, the provincial government building, on the main road through Porto Maurizio. Nobody has published when it was planted or how old it is. If you know, tell us.

Our pin is the register's point. The tree is tall enough to see from the street, and seeing it costs nothing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height and shape, a straight 26-metre trunk with a dense dark dome of stiff, prickly leaves, beside the Palazzo della Provincia at Viale Matteotti 147.
trees.access: Free: visible from Viale Matteotti at the Palazzo della Provincia; the grounds belong to the provincial offices.
trees.transport: In Imperia (Porto Maurizio), about 7 km straight line from Pontedassio; buses run along Viale Matteotti.

trees.name: The Hackberry of San Michele, Diano Borello

location.address: Chiesa di San Michele Arcangelo, Diano Borello, Diano Arentino

trees.story:
A hackberry five metres round is a big one: this species is planted in squares and by churches all over the Mediterranean, and most never come close. Italy's national list of monumental trees measures this one at 5.1 metres round and 15 metres tall, at the parish church of San Michele Arcangelo in Diano Borello.

The church stands on a promontory above the Diano valley, on a cobbled churchyard. Over its door a fresco of Saint Michael between Saint Peter and Saint John the Baptist carries the date 11 June 1485 in Roman numerals, and the stone balls on the facade are, by local tradition, the remains of a temple to Diana that gave the valley its name.

The hackberry is the classic shade tree of Mediterranean squares, with smooth grey bark like an elephant's skin, leaves with a long pointed tip, and small dark berries that birds love. Nobody has published how old this one is. If you know, tell us.

Our pin is the register's point. It costs nothing to see, and the view over the valley from the churchyard is worth the stop as well.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its thick trunk of smooth grey bark, more than five metres round, at the cobbled churchyard of San Michele Arcangelo on the promontory of Diano Borello.
trees.access: Free: the churchyard of the parish church of San Michele Arcangelo.
trees.transport: In the hills behind Diano Marina, about 5 km straight line from Pontedassio; by car is easiest.

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), no. 01/D293/IM/07

Riviera dei Fiori DMO page on Diano Arentino (rivieradeifiori.travel/en/?p=32150): San Michele Arcangelo on a cobblestone churchyard on the promontory of Diano Borello, fresco over the portal dated 11 June 1485, stone spheres said to be the head of Diana; it does not mention the tree. Tree facts single register source: flagged.

trees.name: The Downy Oaks of Maro Castello

location.address: Prato della Corte, Maro Castello, Borgomaro

trees.story:
These two oaks are listed together on Italy's national list of monumental trees, a few metres apart in the meadow called Prato della Corte at Maro Castello, and the list gives them the same measurements: 3.32 metres round and 19 metres tall each.

Maro Castello is a hamlet of Borgomaro, high in the Impero valley, named for the castle of Maro, now in ruins after it was destroyed in battle. Borgomaro itself is an odd one among Ligurian villages, laid out on a grid like a chessboard instead of in rings, and the valley is known for its rare Conio beans.

The downy oak is the oak of dry Mediterranean hillsides, named for the soft hairs on the underside of its young leaves and shoots. It holds its dead brown leaves through much of the winter, so even in January the pair will not look bare. Nobody has published how old they are. If you know, tell us.

Our pin is the register's point, and we could not confirm whether the meadow itself is open, so look from the lane if you are unsure. Seeing them costs nothing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as a matched pair of broad oaks about 19 metres tall, standing together in the Prato della Corte meadow at the hamlet of Maro Castello.
trees.access: Free to see from the lane; the meadow is called Prato della Corte, and we could not confirm whether it is open ground.
trees.transport: Up the Impero valley, about 5 km straight line west of Pontedassio; by car is easiest.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of the Lampedusa Sanctuary, Castellaro

location.address: Santuario di Nostra Signora di Lampedusa, Castellaro

trees.story:
The sanctuary this holm oak stands beside was founded on an escape story. In 1561, the legend goes, a man from Castellaro named Andrea Anfosso was captured by Turkish raiders and taken to the island of Lampedusa, broke free, built a makeshift boat and sailed home using a painting of the Madonna as his sail. That image is still venerated inside.

The path up to the sanctuary climbs through old holm oaks, and Italy's national list of monumental trees picks out this one at the sanctuary itself: 3.65 metres round and 13 metres tall. The writer Giovanni Ruffini set a scene of his nineteenth-century novel Il Dottor Antonio here, so you can compare his descriptions with the hill as it is now.

The holm oak is the evergreen oak of the Mediterranean, with dark, leathery leaves that are grey and felted underneath, and in a dry place like this hilltop it grows slowly. Nobody has published how old this one is. If you know, tell us.

Our pin is the register's point. It stands at a place of pilgrimage open to all, and seeing it costs nothing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its broad evergreen crown of dark, leathery leaves and a thick trunk more than three and a half metres round, beside the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lampedusa on the hilltop above Castellaro.
trees.access: Free: at the sanctuary, reached by road or by the footpath up from Castellaro.
trees.transport: In the hills between Taggia and Sanremo, about 13 km straight line from Pontedassio; by car is easiest.

It does not single out this tree. Flagged, single register source for the tree. HELD 2026-10-20: written and ready, kept off the page only by the 60-trees-in-24-hours pace cap; publish the next day.

trees.name: The Chestnut of the Passo Furchè, Ceriana

location.address: Passo Furchè, on the ridge road above Ceriana

trees.story:
Eight and a half metres round and only five metres tall: that is how Italy's national list of monumental trees measures this sweet chestnut on the Passo Furchè, a pass on the mountain ridge above Ceriana. A trunk that thick on a tree that short is the shape of a very old chestnut that has lost its top and kept going.

A mountain-bike guide to the ridge route calls it a 1,300-year-old chestnut and says it is worth the trip on its own. Nobody has measured its age, and a Swiss survey of monumental chestnuts warns that girth is a poor clock: a trunk of eight metres could mean anything from three to seven centuries. So we leave the age open and let the trunk speak.

Ceriana sits among chestnut woods, olive groves and flower fields in the upper Armea valley, and this tree stands high above it, on the dirt ridge road that runs under the Fascia d'Ubaga towards Monte Furchè.

Getting here is part of the trip: a long climb by car or bike, then gravel. It stands on open mountain land and costs nothing to see.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, enormous and squat, eight and a half metres round but only about five metres tall, beside the gravel ridge road at the Passo Furchè.
trees.access: Free: open mountain land beside the ridge road; the last stretch is a gravel track.
trees.transport: On the ridge above Ceriana, about 17 km straight line from Pontedassio; by car on a long climb, the last part gravel.

Gulliver.it MTB route 'Furchè (Cima) da Bussana' (baloo, 2013, revised 2026-10-01): 'al passo e Monte Furchè dove c'è un castagno di 1300 anni che vale il viaggio', photo captioned 'il castagno di 1300 anni', on the sterrata di dorsale under the Fascia d'Ubaga; route summit 1033 m. trees.name: The Horse Chestnuts of Sant'Agostino, Triora
trees.story:
Triora is famous for its witches. In 1588 women of this mountain village were accused of witchcraft, inquisitors came from Genoa, and the trials dragged on for years; the village is known as the site of the last witch trials held in Italy, and keeps the story alive with a museum and a festival. Its trees are a quieter reason to come.

Two horse chestnuts stand by the church of Sant'Agostino, and Italy's national list of monumental trees records both: one 3.9 metres round and 24.5 metres tall, the other 3.62 metres round and 28 metres tall. That is tall for trees in a mountain village.

The horse chestnut comes from the mountains of the Balkans and was planted all over Europe for its shade and its spring candles of white flowers, which come out here in May. In autumn the shiny brown conkers drop from their spiky cases, and the leaves turn yellow and rust.

A third listed horse chestnut stands at the church of San Bernardino, a few hundred metres away. Nobody has published how old any of them are. If you know, tell us. They stand by a church and cost nothing to see.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as two tall horse chestnuts with big hand-shaped leaves of five to seven leaflets, standing together by the church of Sant'Agostino in Triora.
trees.access: Free: beside the church of Sant'Agostino.
trees.transport: In Triora, high in the Argentina valley, about 19 km straight line from Pontedassio; by car up the valley from Arma di Taggia, or the bus from Sanremo.

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), nos. 01/L430/IM/07 and 02/L430/IM/07

trees.verify_notes: MASAF register 01/L430/IM/07: Aesculus hippocastanum, Triora, Chiesa di Sant'Agostino, girth 390 cm, height 24.5 m, 43.994797, 7.762883; 02/L430/IM/07 same church, girth 362 cm, height 28 m, 43.994867, 7.763064 (about 17 m apart): one collectible point; height field 28 is the taller of the two, girth left out of the field. Triora: site of the last witch trials held in Italy (en.wikipedia Triora); accusations in 1588, inquisitors from Genoa, museum of ethnology and witchcraft, Strigora festival (ligurialetters.substack.com, 2023). borghidiriviera.it lists Sant'Agostino among Triora's churches; no source beyond the register mentions the trees. Bus from Sanremo up the Valle Argentina exists (Riviera Trasporti line to Triora) per general knowledge, not checked this pass. Flagged.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of San Bernardino, Triora
trees.story:
The church of San Bernardino is dedicated to Saint Bernardino of Siena, who came to preach in Triora around 1418, and its walls carry fifteenth-century frescoes, among them a Last Judgement crowded with demons, women in mitres and heretics in the flames. Outside it, Italy's national list of monumental trees records a horse chestnut 3.1 metres round and 20 metres tall.

It is the smaller of Triora's three listed horse chestnuts; the other two stand together by the church of Sant'Agostino, a few hundred metres away, so all three make one short walk. The witch trials that began here in 1588 are told in the village's Museum of Ethnology and Witchcraft.

The horse chestnut is a mountain tree from the Balkans, planted across Europe for its shade. In May it carries upright candles of white flowers flecked with pink and yellow, and in autumn it drops shiny brown conkers from spiky cases, while its big hand-shaped leaves turn yellow and rust.

Nobody has published how old it is. If you know, tell us. It stands by a church and costs nothing to see.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big horse chestnut beside the church of San Bernardino in Triora, with large hand-shaped leaves of five to seven leaflets.
trees.access: Free: beside the church of San Bernardino.
trees.transport: In Triora, about 360 m from the Sant'Agostino horse chestnuts.

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), no. 04/L430/IM/07

trees.verify_notes: MASAF register 04/L430/IM/07: Aesculus hippocastanum, Triora, Chiesa di San Bernardino, girth 310 cm, height 20 m, 43.991728, 7.763914. ligurialetters.substack.com (2023, read in full): San Bernardino dedicated to Bernardino of Siena, who came to Triora around 1418; fifteenth-century frescoes including Il Giudizio Universale with demonic creatures, women wearing mitres and heretics being burned; Museo etnografico e della Stregoneria; accusations in 1588. A search summary (visititaly.eu) calls it a small church somewhat outside the village surrounded by greenery (lead only, not in the story). Flagged, single register source for the tree.
